Creeds and Confessions
kreedz and kun-FESH-unz
noun phrase
From Latin credo (I believe; the opening word of the Nicene and Apostles’ Creeds) and Latin confessio (a declaration, acknowledgment, public statement), from confiteri (to acknowledge, declare openly). Together the terms name the church’s two major genres of subordinate doctrinal standards: brief summary confessions of essential faith (creeds) and fuller systematic expositions of a tradition’s doctrinal commitments (confessions).

Biblical Definition

Creeds and confessions are the church’s subordinate standards—instruments by which the body of Christ gives public, ordered expression to what it believes, teaches, and confesses from Scripture, and by which it guards the flock against doctrinal deviation. The practice of creedal formulation is biblical in instinct: the church is commanded to contend earnestly for “the faith once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 3), to “hold fast the pattern of sound words” (2 Tim. 1:13), and to have elders who are able to teach and exhort by “sound doctrine” and to refute those who contradict (Titus 1:9). Creedal summaries appear in Scripture itself: the Shema (Deut. 6:4), the earliest Christological confessions (“Jesus is Lord,” Rom. 10:9; 1 Cor. 12:3), and Paul’s gospel summary in 1 Corinthians 15:3–5. The historic creeds—Apostles’, Nicene (381), Chalcedonian (451), Athanasian—represent the church’s conciliar definition of Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy against specific heresies. The Reformation confessions—Augsburg (1530), Helvetic Confessions, Heidelberg Catechism (1563), Belgic Confession (1561), Canons of Dort (1618–19), Westminster Confession (1647), and the 1689 London Baptist Confession—represent fuller systematic statements of Protestant doctrine that subordinate standards serve in their proper role: not as authorities equal to Scripture but as faithful summaries of what Scripture teaches, binding the churches that receive them under Scripture’s own authority. The 1689 Baptist Confession (1.10) explicitly names Scripture as “the supreme judge” and all councils and confessions as subordinate to it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Creed: a brief summary of the articles of Christian faith; a formal statement of religious belief. Confession: a formal declaration of religious belief adopted by a church or denomination as its standard of doctrine.

expand to see more

CREED, noun. A brief summary of the articles of Christian faith; a formula containing the fundamental points of religion, designed to be committed to memory.

2. (Theology) The Apostles' Creed, the Nicene Creed, and the Athanasian Creed—the three ecumenical creeds received by all orthodox Christians as faithful summaries of Trinitarian and Christological doctrine.

CON-FES'SION, noun. (Ecclesiastical) A formal declaration of religious belief; a doctrinal standard adopted by a church or council—as the Confession of Augsburg, the Westminster Confession, or the 1689 Baptist Confession.

4. Distinguished from a creed by greater comprehensiveness—confessions typically address not only Trinity and Christology but soteriology, ecclesiology, sacraments, and polity in systematic detail.

Webster's clarity that creeds and confessions are summaries—not authorities in themselves but faithful distillations of Scripture’s teaching—reflects the Protestant doctrine of their subordinate but genuine authority.

Key Scripture

Jude 3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

2 Timothy 1:13 — "Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus."

Titus 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

1 Timothy 6:12 — "Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses."

Modern Corruption

Low-church anti-creedalism (“no creed but the Bible”) in practice replaces tested confessional orthodoxy with the pastor’s individual opinion, leaving congregations with no public standard to which teachers can be held accountable and no inherited wisdom to guard against doctrinal novelty.

expand to see more

The slogan “no creed but the Bible” sounds like sola Scriptura but is actually its inversion. Sola Scriptura affirms that Scripture alone is the supreme and final authority; creeds and confessions are subordinate standards that faithfully summarize Scripture’s teaching and thereby make the church’s publicly professed doctrine legible, testable, and heritable. “No creed but the Bible” in practice means: no public standard, no accountability for what the pastor actually teaches, no inherited wisdom from centuries of hard-won doctrinal definition, and no protection for the congregation against whatever heterodoxy the current leadership may drift toward. Every sect that has fractured from historic orthodoxy has done so by rejecting the confessional deposit—not by submitting more fully to Scripture but by insulating their novelties from Scripture’s tested interpreters.

The opposite error is confessionalism as an authority independent of Scripture—treating the Westminster Confession or the 1689 as infallible in the way Rome treats papal definitions, beyond critique or revision. Reformation confessionalism has always been self-consciously provisional: these are the best summaries we have been given by God’s grace, faithful to Scripture as we understand it, binding on those who receive them, but always open to correction by Scripture itself (1689, 1.10). The goal of creeds and confessions is not to replace Scripture’s authority but to make its teaching stable, teachable, and defensible across generations.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin credo (I believe) and confiteor (I confess, I declare openly) both name the public, corporate act of faith-declaration by which the church puts its doctrine on record before God and the world.

expand to see more

Latin credo — I believe; the first-person singular that opens both the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds, indicating that creeds are personal confessions made in community

Latin confessio — declaration, acknowledgment; from confiteri (to confess, acknowledge openly); the genre of fuller doctrinal standards like the Westminster and 1689

Greek homologia — confession, agreement; used in Heb. 4:14 for holding fast our confession and in 1 Tim. 6:12 for the good confession before witnesses

Latin symbolum — token, symbol; the early church's term for the creed as a “watchword” distinguishing orthodox from heretic, used already in Tertullian

Latin norma normata — normed norm; the Reformation's technical phrase for subordinate standards: they are norms for the church, but they are themselves normed by Scripture (the norma normans)

Usage

"The three ecumenical creeds (Apostles', Nicene, Athanasian) represent the minimum Trinitarian-Christological consensus of all orthodox Christianity; Reformation confessions add soteriology, ecclesiology, and sacramentology with greater precision appropriate to the post-Reformation church's doctrinal context."

"Creeds and confessions are instruments of accountability: a church that adopts the 1689 Baptist Confession publicly commits to Reformed soteriology, believer's baptism by immersion, congregational polity, and the regulative principle—and its members and ministers can be held to that standard."

"The Puritan tradition understood catechesis (the Westminster Shorter Catechism, Spurgeon's adaptation) as the primary vehicle for transmitting confessional content to each new generation—a practice the contemporary church has nearly abandoned at great cost to its doctrinal coherence."
